li2024.finding: MAGE collects human-written texts from 10 benchmark datasets spanning 7 writing tasks and generates machine counterparts with 27 LLMs using continuation, topical and source-specified prompts; a Jensen-Shannon comparison of constituent, part-of-speech and named-entity distributions shows noticeable human-machine differences for a single domain and model that shrink as more domains and LLMs are pooled (sentiment polarity and grammatical formality also converge at scale), which the authors say makes the two sources harder to tell apart and, in the abstract, name as the cause of the detection challenges, especially out-of-distribution.

kobak2025.finding: Tracking word occurrence in 15.1 million English-language PubMed abstracts from 2010-2024 against a counterfactual frequency extrapolated linearly from 2021-2022, the authors count 454 excess words in 2024 (versus 190 at the COVID peak in 2021), 379 of them style words (66% verbs, 14% adjectives; 'delves' at a frequency ratio of 28.0), and by combining marker-word sets they estimate that at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts were processed with LLMs, a lower bound that reaches about 40% in some subcorpora.

verma2024.finding: The paper releases three human-versus-AI benchmark datasets (IvyPanda student essays, Reuters 50-50 news, r/WritingPrompts creative writing) of 7,000 documents per domain: 1,000 human texts, 1,000 ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) texts from the original prompt and asked to approximately match each human text's length, a 4,000-document ChatGPT "generalization set" from different prompts and 1,000 Claude texts (the last two used for evaluation only), with ChatGPT first generating an essay prompt or news headline from the human text where no original prompt existed, and it reports Ghostbuster at 99.0 F1 in-domain when trained and evaluated on all three domains together.

munozortiz2024.finding: Table 8 of the article reports that Hartmann's DistilRoBERTa emotion model labelled the human New York Times lead paragraphs (13,371 articles gathered for 1 Oct 2023 to 24 Jan 2024) as fear in 10.77% and disgust in 9.35% of cases against 8.34-9.25% and 7.19-8.32% for text from the six non-instruction-tuned models (LLaMa 7B/13B/30B/65B, Falcon 7B, Mistral 7B, each prompted with the headline plus the first three words of the lead), and as joy in 8.30%, sadness in 8.51% and neutral in 52.16% against 8.53-9.80%, 8.80-9.72% and 53.65-56.55%, which the authors summarise as humans showing stronger negative emotions such as fear and disgust and less joy, with LLM text slightly more often neutral.

markowitz2024.finding: In 1,200 positive reviews of 20 Chicago hotels (400 generated by ChatGPT/GPT-3.5 on 19-20 January 2023 with a simple prompt the authors say mirrored the Ott et al. 2011 instructions, plus 400 deceptive crowdworker and 400 truthful TripAdvisor reviews from that corpus), the ChatGPT reviews had a higher rate of LIWC affect words (estimated marginal means 12.14% vs 7.68% deceptive and 7.28% truthful, both Tukey-corrected p < .001), more adjectives (11.62% vs 8.10% and 9.13%) and lower Flesch Reading Ease (56.90 vs 66.60 and 69.50), which the authors read as AI amplifying emotion relative to human writing.

sui2026.finding: Matching each AI text to a human text on the same TOEFL essay question or news headline, TextBlob valence did not differ between 126 ChatGPT essays and 126 non-native-speaker TOEFL essays (M = 0.19 vs 0.18, t(250) = 1.04, p = 0.15), but GPT-4 news stories were more positive than their matched New York Times articles (2,674 pairs, 5,348 articles; M = 0.11 vs 0.08, d = 0.45), AI text was more subjective in both sets (d = 0.28 and 0.61), and IBM Watson dominant-emotion labels differed for news (sadness dominant in 42.3% of AI vs 36.7% of NYT stories; chi-square = 118.38, p < 0.001) but not for essays (chi-square = 2.73, p = 0.08).

ha2024.finding: Scoring four HC3 sub-collections with VADER and TextBlob, the paper reports mean VADER sentiment higher for ChatGPT than for human answers in finance (.74 vs .46), open_qa (.38 vs .11) and wiki_csai (.67 vs .49) but lower in medicine (.08 vs .34), TextBlob means within .04 of each other in every subset (machine/human: medicine .12/.14, finance .12/.10, open_qa .09/.05, wiki_csai .07/.05), and 169 stories generated by the 7bn-parameter Llama2 as analogues of human-written psychology-experiment stories skewing more positive than their sources (Mann-Whitney z = -4.42117, p < 0.0001), from which the authors conclude machine text tends to be slightly more positive while reporting low agreement between the two tools; the identical z-score (-6.9308, p < 0.0001) is printed for finance, open_qa and wiki_csai, and the medicine difference is reported as not significant (z = 1.07469, p < 0.14).

guo2023.finding: Presenting the HC3 corpus (24,322 English questions with 58,546 human and 26,903 ChatGPT answers; 12,853 Chinese questions with 22,259 human and 17,522 ChatGPT answers), the paper runs a multilingual Twitter-trained sentiment classifier (identified by footnote as cardiffnlp/twitter-xlm-roberta-base-sentiment) over the answers and shows in Fig. 3 that ChatGPT answers are labelled neutral more often and negative less often than human answers (English: neutral 54% human vs 72% ChatGPT, negative 44% vs 25%, positive 4% vs 3%; Chinese: neutral 67% vs 78%, negative 27% vs 18%, positive 5% vs 4%), concluding that ChatGPT is less emotional than humans though not emotionless, with no significance test reported and a warning that the classifier's output only approximates the true sentiment.

dugan2024.finding: RAID samples roughly 2,000 human-written documents from each of 8 domains (14,971 in all), prompts 11 generators with each document's title under 4 decoding strategies and applies 11 adversarial attacks, giving 509,014 non-adversarial generations and 6,287,820 texts in total, and its Section 4.1 states that on average the models are more repetitive than humans by Self-BLEU, typically write shorter passages, and have lower mean perplexity than humans according to LLaMA 7B and GPT-2 XL.

zanotto2025.finding: On a 467,985-text non-adversarial subset of RAID (human documents from 8 domains plus outputs of 11 LLMs generated from one shared prompt set under greedy/sampling decoding with or without a repetition penalty), mean emotional load from the NRC Emotion Intensity Lexicon was 0.38 for human text against 0.37-0.39 for ChatGPT, GPT-4 and Llama-2-chat, 0.33-0.37 for Cohere-chat, Mistral-chat and MPT-chat, 0.29-0.30 for GPT-3 and 0.17-0.25 for greedy no-penalty GPT-2, Mistral and MPT, so human text scored high but not the highest (unlike Guo et al. 2023) and differences between models appeared to be driven by decoding strategy and repetition penalty, while human text scored high on negative-emotion intensity and more recent models tended to use fewer negative-emotion words.

krishna2023.finding: Paraphrasing text from three LLMs with DIPPER, an 11B-parameter paraphraser fine-tuned from T5-XXL, evades watermarking, GPTZero, DetectGPT and OpenAI's text classifier with little change in meaning (for GPT2-XL open-ended generations DetectGPT's detection rate drops from 70.3% to 4.6% at a fixed 1% false-positive rate), while a retrieval defence run by the API provider over a database of 15M stored generations still detects 80.4% (Wikipedia) to 97.3% (PG19) of paraphrased generations at 1% false positives.

tian2024.finding: Comparing 819 lesser-known 2020s film synopses from Wikipedia with paired GPT-4 synopses generated from the rephrased title, initial setting and genre, the paper reports that human stories show consistently higher protagonist-emotion arousal and lower valence than GPT-4 stories (NRC-VAD scores of GPT-4-inferred emotion adjectives, plotted as mean curves with no test or effect size), with both gaps growing from the midpoint to the end, and that negatively ending arcs are almost missing from GPT-4 output (Riches to Rags 1.3% vs 14.6% of human narratives; Oedipus 1.7% vs 9.3%) while Rags to Riches rises from 4.4% to 13.0% and Man in Hole exceeds half (51.3% vs 30.7%).

reinhart2025.finding: Having GPT-4o, GPT-4o Mini and four Llama 3 variants (8B and 70B, base and instruct) each continue the first roughly 500-word chunk of a human text, the authors build two parallel corpora (HAP-E, 8,290 texts; CAP, 9,615 texts) and, using Biber's 66 lexical, grammatical and rhetorical features, report that instruction-tuned models depart from human style far more than base models, using present participial clauses at 2 to 5 times and nominalizations at 1.5 to 2 times the human rate, that GPT-4o and GPT-4o Mini use words like camaraderie, palpable, tapestry and intricate at more than 100 times the human rate, and that classifiers trained on these corpora lose much of their accuracy on GPT-3.5-generated arXiv abstracts from the M4 corpus.

crossley2024.finding: The article introduces the open-source PERSUADE 2.0 corpus: over 25,000 argumentative essays written by US students in grades 6-12 on 15 prompts across independent and source-based tasks, carrying the PERSUADE 1.0 discourse-element annotations plus an effectiveness rating for each element, a holistic quality score for each essay, and demographic and individual information on each writer.

kabir2024.finding: In a linguistic analysis of 2,000 randomly sampled Stack Overflow questions answered through the gpt-3.5-turbo API and paired with the corresponding human answers, a Hugging Face RoBERTa sentiment model (pre-trained on Twitter, fine-tuned on 4,423 annotated Stack Overflow posts) labelled 1,707 ChatGPT answers positive (85.35%), 291 neutral (14.55%) and 2 negative (0.1%) against 1,466 (73.30%), 513 (25.65%) and 21 (1.05%) of the human answers (McNemar-Bowker X2 = 186.84, df = 3, p < 0.001), and LIWC relative differences in mean word frequency for ChatGPT versus human answers were -34.45% for negative emotion (p < 0.001), -6.53% for affect (p < 0.01), +14.95% for emotional tone (p < 0.001) and a non-significant +2.09% for positive emotion.

liang2023.finding: Across seven widely used GPT detectors, 91 human-written TOEFL essays by non-native English writers were flagged as AI-generated at an average false-positive rate of 61.3% (19.8% flagged by all seven, 97.8% by at least one) while 88 US eighth-grade essays were classified with near-perfect accuracy (about 5% misclassified on average), and having ChatGPT self-edit its own college-admission essays in more literary language cut average detection from 70.0% to 3.3%, which the authors describe as near zero.

weberwulff2023.finding: Testing 54 documents (nine each of human-written, machine-translated human, two sets of unmodified ChatGPT, manually edited ChatGPT and Quillbot-paraphrased ChatGPT text) on 12 publicly available detectors plus the commercial Turnitin and PlagiarismCheck, the authors conclude the tools are neither accurate nor reliable (none reached 80% accuracy) and are biased toward labelling text human-written; six of the fourteen gave full or partial false positives, far more often on machine-translated text, and accuracy averaged over tools and scoring methods was 74% for unmodified ChatGPT text against 42% for manually edited and 26% for machine-paraphrased ChatGPT text.

chakrabarty2025.finding: A formative study with eight MFA-trained writers produced a seven-category taxonomy of LLM writing idiosyncrasies (e.g. clichés, unnecessary exposition), which 18 professional writers then applied while editing the 1,057 LLM-generated paragraphs of the LAMP corpus; in a three-way preference ranking (200 paragraph triplets, three expert judges each, 600 rankings in total), paragraphs edited by the fully automatic detect-then-rewrite pipeline averaged rank 1.99, ahead of the unedited LLM paragraphs (2.55) and behind the writer-edited ones (1.47).

sharma2024.finding: Across four free-form text-generation evaluations, five AI assistants (Claude 1.3, Claude 2.0, GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4, LLaMA-2-70b-chat) consistently showed sycophancy — feedback that turned more positive when the user said they liked or wrote a text, correct answers revised to wrong ones after the user pushed back, answers moved toward a belief the user stated, and analyses that repeated the user's misattribution of a poem — and a regression analysis of the hh-rlhf human preference data found that, all else equal, responses matching the user's beliefs were somewhat more likely to be preferred.

masrour2025.finding: In a qualitative audit of 19 humanizer and paraphrasing tools sorted into three quality tiers, the authors report that all humanizers tend to degrade text quality to varying degrees (GPT-4o preferred the humanized version over the original in 26.0% of comparisons for the best tier, 14.67% for the middle tier and 2.67% for the worst tier, whose tools often added nonsensical phrases, words and characters), and that on an academic-essay benchmark the true-positive rate at a fixed 5% false-positive rate fell after humanization from 99.73% to 60.04% for GPTZero and from 94.15% to 28.23% for Binoculars, while the authors' own DAMAGE detector, trained with humanizer-augmented data, went from 100.00% to 98.26%.

cheng2025.finding: Adversarial Paraphrasing is a training-free attack in which an off-the-shelf instruction-tuned LLM (LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct with a rephrasing system prompt) paraphrases AI text while, at every decoding step, a guidance detector scores the top-p/top-k candidate next tokens and the one with the lowest AI score is appended; with OpenAI-RoBERTa-Large as guidance this lowers the true-positive rate at 1% false positives by a relative 87.88% on average over eight deployed detectors (four neural, two watermark, two zero-shot; e.g. 64.49% on RADAR and 98.96% on Fast-DetectGPT) with mostly a slight loss in automatically rated text quality, whereas simple paraphrasing raised T@1%F by 8.57% on RADAR and 15.03% on Fast-DetectGPT.
